name: ReAct Loop
question: What should I do next, given what I just saw?
summary: ReAct interleaves reasoning with actions: the model thinks, calls a tool, reads the observation and decides again, until it can answer. Because every step sees the latest result, it copes with paths nobody could predict. It is the default loop in most agent SDKs, and it needs a step cap, compact tool results and errors returned as observations.
useCases: The next step depends on what the last tool returned
Diagnosis and investigation tasks with branching paths
A small, well-described tool set the model can choose from reliably

items.detail: the model reasons about what to do next
the tool’s result, appended to the history
a final answer, or a hard step cap
every call resends all earlier steps
returned to the model as observations, not raised as crashes

steps: Define a few tools with tight schemas and short, informative results
Run the loop: call the model, execute its tool calls, append the results, repeat
Cap the steps and stop gracefully with a partial answer
Log every trace so failures can be replayed and graded
pitfalls: No step cap means loops that never end
Verbose tool results inflate every later call
Re-deciding after every observation is slow and costly for routine tasks
remember: Think, act, observe. Cap the loop.
caption: Each call resends the whole history, so tokens grow with every step. Numbers are illustrative.

steps.title: Define a few tight tools
steps.text: Three tools with short descriptions and strict input schemas. The model can only act through them, so clear names and required fields matter more than clever prompts.

steps.title: Think, then act
steps.text: The model reads the question and replies with a tool call rather than an answer: get_order for order 8812. The stop reason tool_use tells your loop to run it.

steps.title: Observe the result
steps.text: Your code runs the tool and appends the result as a tool_result message: “shipped”. That observation is what the next step reasons about.

steps.title: Loop with the growing history
steps.text: The model is called again with everything so far and asks for the courier status: “held at hub”. Each call resends the whole history, so input grows from 1.2k to 3.4k to 5.8k tokens.

steps.title: Stop on an answer or the cap
steps.text: On the third call the model answers instead of calling a tool, so the loop ends after 3 of the 8 allowed steps. If the cap is reached first, the loop stops and hands over.

steps.title: Return errors as observations
steps.text: When the courier API times out, the loop returns “error: timeout” as the tool result. The model retries or picks another route instead of the whole run crashing.

pros: Handles paths nobody can predict, one observation at a time
The default loop in most agent SDKs, so little code
Recovers from tool errors when they come back as observations
Traces are easy to read, replay and grade
cons: Every call resends the growing history, so tokens compound
Re-decides after every step, which is slow for routine work
Can loop or stall without a cap
Quality depends heavily on tool design and result size
avoidWhen: The steps are known in advance (use a workflow)
The steps are knowable but deciding each one is costly (use plan-and-execute)

playgroundGuide.scenario: A telecom operator's support agent diagnoses why a customer's SIM swap failed. The next check depends on what the last tool returned, so the model runs a ReAct loop: think, call a tool, read the result, decide again. You control the step cap, how tool errors are handled, how big each tool result is, and whether the provisioning tool is flaky.
controls: Drag the slider to set the step cap (maximum model calls).
Choose full or compact tool results, and tick whether errors come back to the model as observations.
Tick the flaky tool to make the provisioning log time out once, or load a scenario.

outputs.name: Total tokens
outputs.meaning: All input and output tokens across the run. Each call resends the whole history.

outputs.name: Latency
outputs.meaning: About 1.5 s per model call and 0.4 s per tool call.

practice.scenario: A telecom operator's support agent diagnoses failed SIM swaps. Nobody can list the steps in advance: the next check depends on whether the swap request exists, whether KYC re-verification passed and whether the network provisioning job errored. A ReAct loop with four tools, a step cap of 8 and compact tool results handles it, and every trace is logged for grading.

industries.use: Diagnose SIM swaps, porting failures and recharge issues step by step
Investigate an incident by querying logs, then metrics, then recent deploys
Trace a rejected order through margin, RMS and exchange responses

practice.analogy: A doctor taking a history. Each answer decides the next question; nobody hands the doctor a fixed list.

library.name: OpenAI Agents SDK
library.what: A small agent framework whose Runner executes the tool loop for you, with max_turns as the step cap and tracing built in.

practice.note: The tool bodies are stubs; connect them to your own systems. MaxTurnsExceeded is raised when the cap is hit.

numericDrill.question: In a ReAct loop the system prompt and tools take 2,000 tokens, and each step adds 800 tokens (the tool call and its result). Step n therefore sends 2,000 + 800 × (n − 1) input tokens. How many input tokens do 6 steps send in total?
numericDrill.answer: The fixed part is 6 × 2,000 = 12,000. The growing part is 800 × (0 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5) = 800 × 15 = 12,000. Total 24,000 input tokens, twice what 6 independent calls would send.

interview.question: Why should tool errors be returned to the model instead of raised?
interview.answer: An error message is an observation the model can act on: retry with different arguments, use another tool or tell the user. Raising an exception ends the run and throws away the progress so far. Keep the error short and specific so it helps the next step.

interview.question: How do you stop a ReAct agent from looping?
interview.answer: Set a hard step cap, such as max_turns, and stop gracefully with a partial answer or a hand-off. Make tool results informative so the model does not repeat calls, and log traces to find the tools or prompts that cause loops.

mistakes.mistake: Returning full API payloads as observations
mistakes.fix: Return only the fields the next decision needs

mistakes.mistake: Running a loop with no step cap
mistakes.fix: Cap the steps and define what happens when the cap is hit

quiz.question: A support agent diagnosing failed SIM swaps needs different checks depending on what each lookup returns. Which architecture fits?
options: A fixed prompt chain
A ReAct loop with a step cap
A single call with a large thinking budget
Voting across three prompts
quiz.explanation: When the next step depends on the last observation, a ReAct loop fits; the cap keeps it bounded.

quiz.question: A ReAct agent keeps calling get_order with the same id until it hits the cap. Traces show the tool message contains the arguments, not the result. What is wrong?
options: The step cap is too low
The observation never reaches the model
The model is too small
The tool schema is too strict
quiz.explanation: If the tool result is not appended, the model never sees the outcome and repeats the call.

quiz.question: The system prompt and tools take 2,000 tokens, each step adds 800, and step n sends 2,000 + 800 × (n − 1) input tokens. How many input tokens do 6 steps send in total?
A tool that checks card status sometimes times out, and each timeout crashes the whole agent run. What change keeps runs alive?
options: Raise the step cap
Return the error to the model as a tool result
Use a larger model
Remove the tool
quiz.explanation: Returned as an observation, the error lets the model retry or choose another route instead of ending the run.

quiz.question: A broker’s order-investigation agent burns tokens on long traces. Which changes reduce tokens per task? Select all that apply.
options: Return only the fields the next step needs from each tool
Load only the tools relevant to the task
Raise the step cap from 8 to 20
Add more example traces to the system prompt
quiz.explanation: Compact results and fewer tool definitions shrink every call. A higher cap and longer prompts increase tokens.

quiz.question: With the OpenAI Agents SDK, what happens when an agent run exceeds max_turns?
options: The run silently returns the last message
MaxTurnsExceeded is raised
The SDK doubles the limit
The model is switched to a smaller one
quiz.explanation: The Runner raises MaxTurnsExceeded once the turn limit is passed, so you can stop gracefully or hand off.

quiz.question: A clinical-coding agent’s tool returns the full 6,000-token patient record on every lookup, and later calls get slow. Why do later calls suffer most?
options: The model gets tired
Every later call resends all earlier tool results
Tools run slower over time
The cap counts tokens
quiz.explanation: ReAct history grows with each step, so a large early result is paid for again on every later call.

quiz.question: Which elements make up one ReAct step? Select all that apply.
options: A thought about what to do next
An action: a tool call with arguments
An observation: the tool result fed back
A fixed plan written before the task starts
quiz.explanation: ReAct interleaves thought, action and observation. A plan written up front is plan-and-execute.

quiz.question: A claims-status agent needs 5 model calls on a normal task and 6 when one tool retry happens. What is the smallest step cap that handles the retry case?
quiz.explanation: The cap must cover the calls the task needs, here 6 with a retry. Anything lower stops the run early.

quiz.question: Compared with 6 independent calls of 2,000 tokens each, how much more input does a 6-step ReAct loop send if each step adds 800 tokens of history?
options: 12,000 more
4,800 more
9,600 more
None
quiz.explanation: Independent calls: 12,000. ReAct: 24,000 (see the growing history). The loop sends 12,000 more.

quiz.question: A ReAct agent loops on some tasks. Which safeguards belong in production? Select all that apply.
options: A hard step cap with a graceful hand-off
Logging every trace for replay and grading
Removing all error handling so failures are visible
Letting the model decide when the cap applies
quiz.explanation: Caps and traces keep loops bounded and debuggable. Crashing on errors and letting the model control the cap defeat the purpose.

quiz.question: A bank’s standard address-change process always runs the same four steps. A team built it as a ReAct agent and it costs three times its budget. What should they do?
options: Raise the budget
Replace it with a fixed workflow
Add reflection
Add tree search
quiz.explanation: Re-deciding after every observation is wasted on a fixed procedure; a workflow runs the same steps far more cheaply.

quiz.question: Which smolagents class do its agents build on, as “an abstraction of ReAct framework”?
options: ToolCallingChain
MultiStepAgent
PlannerAgent
ReActGraph
quiz.explanation: smolagents documents MultiStepAgent as the ReAct abstraction that its agents build on.

quiz.question: On ALFWorld and WebShop, how did ReAct compare with imitation and reinforcement learning baselines in the original paper?
options: It was 34 and 10 absolute points better
It matched them
It was worse on both
It was only tested on HotpotQA
quiz.explanation: The paper reports gains of 34 and 10 absolute points with only one or two in-context examples.

quiz.question: An EdTech tutor agent answers from a course-search tool. Which tool-result designs help the loop? Select all that apply.
options: Short results with the fields the model needs
Clear error messages that suggest a next step
Raw HTML pages of the course site
Identical wording for success and failure
quiz.explanation: Compact, informative results and helpful errors let the model decide well. Raw HTML bloats context and ambiguous results cause repeats.

quiz.question: A dispute agent makes 5 calls. Input per call is 1,200 tokens plus 220 tokens for each earlier step, and each call writes 100 output tokens. What is the total token count?
A ReAct agent sometimes answers after 3 steps even though the cap is 8. Is this a problem?
options: Yes: it should use all 8
No: the cap is a limit, and it stopped because it had an answer
Yes: caps must equal the steps used
No: caps are ignored by the model
quiz.explanation: The loop ends when the model answers without a tool call. The cap only bounds runaway cases.

quiz.question: Why did ReAct reduce hallucination on HotpotQA and FEVER compared with reasoning alone?
options: It used a larger model
It grounded reasoning in results from a Wikipedia API
It removed chain of thought
It used voting
quiz.explanation: Interleaving reasoning with lookups let the model check facts against retrieved results instead of inventing them.

quiz.question: A fleet-tracking agent has 25 tools loaded and often picks the wrong one. Which fixes are sensible? Select all that apply.
options: Load only the tools relevant to the task
Give tools distinct names and clear descriptions
Raise the temperature
Add more tools so the right one is always present
quiz.explanation: Fewer, clearly described tools make selection easier and shrink every call. Temperature and more tools make it worse.

quiz.question: A ReAct agent at a brokerage must never place trades without approval. Where should that control sit?
options: In the system prompt only
In code: the place_order tool requires an approval step before it runs
In the step cap
In the model’s thinking budget
quiz.explanation: Safety-critical controls belong in code around the tool, not in instructions the model might ignore.
